rewrite: Consider that Earth has been sculpting itself for exactly 4.5 billion years—a span so vast that the entire arc of human civilization, from the first crude settlements along the Euphrates to the digital networks encircling the globe, occupies less than the final ten-thousandth of one percent of that history. Long before any person observed them, supercontinents merged and fractured, seas expanded and contracted, and peaks ascended only to be eroded into silt. Countless organisms rose to prominence and eventually disappeared, leaving behind nothing but subtle chemical traces embedded in geological strata. Even the iron circulating in our veins originated within dying stars prior to the planet's formation from cosmic debris. In this context, our most lasting structures, ancient scripts, and established systems are merely transient sparks during an eternal tempest. This immense scale of time is not an act of malice, but a reminder of how unlikely our existence is and that the world's narrative is not centered on humanity. We have arrived late, resting upon a historical abyss that we can categorize but never fully comprehend.
